extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers (Naval Postgraduate School) preparing academic/technical writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formatting numbers, units, and mathematical expressions in academic and technical prose (when to spell numbers, inline vs display math, punctuation of equations, and which style guides to follow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow discipline/style guide norms for numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The various disciplines and style guides have different norms for incorporating numbers into your text; consult style-specific guidance for how to format numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links infographics for major styles (APA, Chicago, IEEE) and states: 'These documents provide useful rules of thumb; consult with your advisor or professor if you have questions about particular points of numerical usage.' Use the relevant style guide's conventions rather than inventing your own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between inline and display mathematics appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions can be placed in-line (surrounded by text) or on their own line as display equations; choose the form that fits the expression and flow of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes: 'There are ∛8 main ways to incorporate mathematics into your text: you can either place it in-line, surrounded by text, or you can place it on its own line—as a display equation.' Use context and readability to decide; consult the GWC video tutorial 'Clarity – Math Expressions' for guidance on making this choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate display equations correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Display equations require proper punctuation as part of the surrounding sentence structure; there is a correct way to punctuate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page asks 'what’s the proper way to punctuate those display equations (and there is, of course, a proper way)?' and directs readers to the GWC infographic 'How to Punctuate Display Equations' and a short video. Follow the punctuation rules shown in those resources so equations read as part of the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format numbers, units, and equations according to established guides
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established documents and guides for detailed rules on numbers, units of measure, and mathematical notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists resources such as 'Writing Numbers, Units of Measure, and Equations' (Blake & Bly), 'Guidelines for Equations, Units, and Mathematical Notation' (Louisiana Tech), 'Mathematical Writing: A Brief Guide' (Tomforde), 'A Guide to Writing Mathematics' (Lee), and books like Higham's 'Handbook of Writing for the Mathematical Sciences'. Consult these for conventions on notation, units, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, consult your advisor or professor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specific numerical or mathematical formatting question is unclear, follow departmental or advisor preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit advice from the page: 'These documents provide useful rules of thumb; consult with your advisor or professor if you have questions about particular points of numerical usage.' Institutional or instructor norms override generic rules of thumb when specified.
